summary:
As a state of the United States, Arizona operates under federal law applying across the country; that national layer is carried on the United States record rather than repeated here.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Arizona in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, describing that group as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. The same assessment names Arizona together with Virginia as a state whose youth-targeting anti-trans policies were judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

No restriction on transgender adults' use of public facilities has been enacted in Arizona. In June 2023 the governor vetoed legislature-passed bills on restroom use and on classroom pronoun usage, and vetoed an April 2023 bill aimed at LGBT safe spaces in schools. Introduced in March 2023, a Department of Education hotline accepts reports on schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology, for investigation.

Arizona's document rules have been shaped by litigation. Three families with transgender children sued the Department of Health Services in November 2020 over birth-certificate gender change without sex reassignment surgery; the case was still running in August 2023 with all resident transgender individuals joined, and in August 2024 a federal judge ordered that change be permitted without surgery. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a signed physician statement attesting that the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, with no surgery required.

Gender-affirming care for adults is not restricted by state law in this record. The surgical restriction the state has enacted applies to minors: a March 2022 statute signed by Governor Doug Ducey bans sex reassignment surgery on transgender children with effect from March 2023, and carries an exception allowing surgery on intersex children. A second March 2022 bill signed by Governor Ducey legally bans transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic-affiliated competition, effective 30 days after enactment.

Arizona's own hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, while it does include sexual orientation, so a bias-motivated crime against a trans person is charged without the state-level penalty enhancement. A gay and trans panic defence remains available at common law, and reform bills have lapsed without action.

This record contains no dated incident of violence targeting a trans person in Arizona, so no pattern of such violence can be established from these sources in either direction.

Coverage in employment, housing and public accommodations rests on a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banning state employment and contract discrimination based on gender identity, a June 2023 Attorney General affirmation that state sex discrimination includes gender identity, and municipal ordinances passed in Phoenix (revised February 2013), Flagstaff (March 2013), Tempe (February 2014), Sedona (2015), Winslow (November 2018), Mesa (March 2021), Scottsdale (April 2021, effective 20 May 2021), Glendale (May 2021) and Tolleson (June 2021). Those ordinances exempt religious organisations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses, so the protection a visitor can rely on varies with the municipality and the type of premises.

Conversion therapy was banned in Pima County by a 3-2 vote in August 2017, with fines of up to 2,500 dollars, and a June 2023 executive order bars government funding for the practice. A statewide statutory ban is not documented.

Marriage for a trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status is recognised here. Same-sex marriage has been recognised since a US district court decision of 17 October 2014 ended enforcement of the statutory and constitutional bans, and those bans remain textually present in the state constitution and in Arizona Revised Statutes, on the Legislature's website, as unenforceable under Obergefell v. Hodges and the federal Respect for Marriage Act of 2022. Voters rejected Proposition 107 in November 2006 and approved Proposition 102 in November 2008, which barred recognition, after which Phoenix, Bisbee, Tucson and Flagstaff enacted domestic partnerships or civil unions.
tangentialFactors:
Tucson Pride cancelled all of its 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; Prism reported on 3 June 2026 that Tucson was grouped with Tampa, Florida and Arlington, Texas as cities where Pride activity was affected. The measure is the fate of an event organisation, not a count of incidents against trans people.

Public opinion polling in the state is dated and does not measure the current climate. A 2017 Public Religion Research Institute survey found 63 per cent of Arizona residents supported same-sex marriage, 73 per cent supported anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 59 per cent opposed religious refusals to serve LGBTQ people; a 2019 PRRI survey found 71 per cent supported LGBTQ non-discrimination legislation. Both survey windows closed years before this record was compiled.

Arizona's placement in the July 2026 Low-Risk States group sits alongside a national picture in which other states have moved in the opposite direction, so the assessment is a comparison across states rather than a statement about conditions inside Arizona in isolation.
localsOnly:
Public health coverage for residents sits under a 1982 regulation providing that Medicaid cannot cover sex reassignment surgery. Two transgender teenagers challenged that regulation in August 2020 with the National Center for Lesbian Rights and the National Health Law Program as unconstitutional, after 2019 lawsuits sought to void the ban. A June 2023 executive order granted Arizona government employees over age 21 full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. How the 1982 regulation and the 2023 order stand against each other is not resolved in these sources.

Adoption is permitted to individuals, with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or on second-parent adoptions; primary consideration goes to married couples unless that is contrary to the child's best interest or no married couple is available. An emergency law signed by Governor Ducey in April 2022 allows religious organisations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster. Surrogacy, gestational or traditional, is prohibited and its contracts are unenforceable, though Soos v. Superior Court (1994) allows pre-birth orders for biological parents, requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent. In September 2017 the Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under Obergefell v. Hodges and Pavan v. Smith to list both names on birth certificates, implemented by an Appeals decision of October 2020. Lesbian couples have IVF access, and state law recognises a non-genetic, non-gestational married mother through donor insemination.

The Arizona Supreme Court ruled on 25 April 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances when divorced parents reach impasse, authorised to decide disputed parenting-plan elements and other factors necessary to emotional and physical health, narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm.

Workplace protection for state employees rests on the January 2023 executive order and the June 2023 Attorney General interpretation; municipal employment and contract ordinances date from a 1992 Phoenix ordinance and a 1999 Tucson ordinance through the 2013 to 2021 expansions listed in the summary.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the 1982 Medicaid regulation barring coverage of sex reassignment surgery and the June 2023 executive order granting state employees full coverage of gender-affirming care are both currently operative, and which governs where they conflict. The sources carry both without reconciling them.

Unresolved: whether the August 2024 federal judge order permitting birth-certificate gender change without surgery has survived appellate review or applies to every petition in the state. The record states the order and the ongoing litigation as of August 2023 and does not track the case further.

Not sourced: any incident of violence against a trans person in Arizona with a date, any state-level figure for such incidents, and any enforcement data on the state hate-crime statute as applied to gender identity. The absence of a dated case here reflects the material available, not a finding that none occurs.

Not sourced: Arizona's legislative pipeline for the current session, whether any facility or adult-targeting bill is pending, and the methodology behind the July 2026 risk grouping.

Unresolved: the scope of the Pima County conversion-therapy ban and the June 2023 funding order beyond government money, since no statewide statutory prohibition on the practice appears in these sources.
